" Dieses Gleichniß soll die Philosophie mit Einem Schlage aus dem Felde schlagen. Die Philosophie antwortet eben so kurz mit [p. 186] dem Zeugnisse des Jüngers, den der Herr lieb hat: So gewiß sich Gott, -das Wort, das da von Anfang war, das Wort des Lebens mit unsern Augen hat beschauen, mit unsern Händen hat betasten lassen, so gewiß entzieht Er sich auch nicht dem Begriffe, wodurch Ihn der Geist, als in Ihm seyend, erkennet. So gewiß Gott in den heiligen Sacramenten nach seiner Verheißung durch ſichtbare und fühlbare Elemente sich mittheilt, und in diesen Elementen sich genießen läßt, so gewiß ist Gott Geist, der im Fleische dem Fleische, als dem Leibe des Geistes, hiermit dem Geiste, dem Begriffe, - nicht dem abſtracten Begriffe -sich wirklich und wesentlich mittheilt. Wo solche Mißverständnisse sich behaupten, und selbst unter den Brüdern in Christo Platz zu nehmen suchen, da sind wohl auch viele und weitläufige Worte nicht überflüssig, um die Identität der speculativen Religionſphiloſophie mit der christlichen Glaubenſerkenntniß in Schutz zu nehmen. Ja, es ist eben jetzt an der Zeit, hierauf im Allgemeinen und im Einzelnen aufmerkſam zu machen, weil eben jetzt die leichten, lofen, falten Zeiten vorüber gehen, welche den ganzen schweren und reichen Gehalt der christlichen Dogmatik und Symbolik, die sich durch alle christliche Jahrhunderte hindurch zieht, auf Erasmische Weise als scholastische Spitzfindigkeiten, als dürre Formeln, und unnütze Grübeleyen zu beseitigen suchten, ohne von der Innigkeit und Treue des Fleißes, von dem unverkennbaren Ernste der Betrachtung, von der Liebe und Tiefe in der Forschung, von der heiligen Scheu und von dem strengen Gehorsame in den steifen Formeln und stehenden Prädicaten im Geringsten berührt zu werden. Aber wer auch nur einzelne Blicke. in diese reiche Geisteswelt gethan hat, der wird bald verwundert stille stehen, und freudig zusehen, wie der Herr durch alle Jahrhunderte seine Kirche baut, und wie zu allen Zeiten Jesu Jünger bey jedem Worte im Worte Gottes verweilen, jedem Fingerzeige nachgehen, an jeder Wahrheit den unerschöpflichen Reichthum nach allen Seiten und nach allen Beziehungen entfalten, in jedem Bilde: [p. 187] außer dessen allgemeiner Bedeutung auch dessen Wirklichkeit verfolgen, die Auslegung nach jedem Sinne, der das Wort selbst unverfälscht stehen läßt, entwickeln, und alle Schätze der Bibel zusammentragen, um das System. bis in die kleinsten Theile, bis in die feinsten Adern auszuführen, , alles, um mehr und mehr, das reiche Wort, als die Kraft Gottes, sich anzueignen, immer tiefer sich hineinzuleben, und mit allen Sinnen in alle Poren immer fester sich einzusaugen. *) Oder sollten wir wirklich noch jetzo meinen, daß ein solcher Umgang mit Gott, weil er zunächst den Gedanken bewegt, das Herz kalt, und die Hände, mit denen wir handeln, träge und ruhig im Schooße liegen lassen sollte. Von allen Worten der heiligen Schrift ist keines überflüssig, denn alle Schrift, von Gott eingegeben, ist nütz zur Lehre, zur Strafe, zur Besserung, zur Züchtigung in der Gerechtigkeit. -So viel zum Frieden zwischen dem Glauben und dem Wissen, welches, als Wissen, der nähern Bezeichnung, als wahres Wissen, entbehren kann, weil alles Wissen wahr ist, wie aller Glaube, denn der Aberglaube, ist nicht Glaube. Demohngeachtet kann der Unterschied zwischen Glauben und Wissen nicht abgeläugnet werden, die Identität schließt den Unterschied nicht aus, und in dem Irrthume, den wir an den Unterschieden nachgewiesen haben, liegt auch Wahrheit; aber dieser Unterschied ist nur nicht so zu fassen, als könnten wir bey seinen Abstractionen stehen.
e: [p. 178] Hence philosophy does not at first interrupt itself with ascetic and parenetic practical application, because these do not fail to appear in the subject if the former is truly understood, and would be of no avail if it is not understood. To be sure, speculation too can prove edifying, as the Epistle of James follows upon the Epistle to the Romans. And where it does not make itself heard in this way, do you know, too, what it quietly works upon the subject, and what this subject, after strict labour under the discipline of the Spirit, who bids it be silent, may confess and make confession of before God upon its knees? Moreover, if in individual branches of philosophy sin is set forth more as darkness than as wickedness, the fault lies in the fragmentation of the different sides of the human spirit, according to which sin too manifests itself, in the intellectual respect, as darkness and blindness. And if, finally, the science of thought finds in sin at first only nullity and emptiness, it must nevertheless go further, and it lies in its very own essence to ask after the ground and essence of this non-essence. And what other answer can come to it than that which is revealed in Scripture? “In that science, through its longing for truth, recognizes the need of love, it also confesses its initial poverty,” poverty in truth and love, “its ignorance” and its lovelessness, or rather this state of affairs with the subject. “It confesses to proceed from nullity, and so it must also openly acknowledge the ground of this nullity of man, amid so much open and hidden wealth, which he does not understand and in his ignorance does not know how to use; it must admit his fall, and must regard God’s condescension to nothingness in order to raise man up again as a self-emptying for man’s sake. [p. 179] Man’s thought too is affected by the Fall; its originally unhindered activity and evidence is hindered, it has fallen into the captivity of representations and feelings, into the power of the so-called associations of ideas; it too needed redemption.” Holy Scripture, to be sure, has proscribed and condemned “the wisdom of this world,” 1 Cor. 1:20–21; 3:19, and “heathen philosophy,” as the “vain deviation according to the teaching of men and the ordinances of the world,” Col. 2:8; but to the wisdom of this world, which the world gives, there is opposed the cognition of the world and its sin, which God gives, and to the philosophy that is empty and vain, and turns away from God, and robs us while it bestows gifts upon us, because it loves human wisdom and world-ordinances, there is opposed that philosophy which loves the wisdom of God, and at the feet of Jesus listens quietly to the foolish preaching of the Gospel, without demanding signs with the Jews, without asking with the Greeks after human wisdom and human proofs. 1 Cor. 1:22–23. 29. [p. 180] Faith teaches us that we are not what we ought to be, but through Him in whom we believe are to become what we are not. With this, being, our being, is condemned, and to the ought is given the prize that is held out to us as the jewel for which we strive. Conversely, however, speculative philosophy holds to the being that is there, and finds, as the science of reason, in actuality and presence the reason that faith regards as otherworldly, as future; with this it releases itself from the burdensome ought, and presses only for cognition of the actual, as of the rational, which is not so impotent as merely to ought and not to be; indeed, it scorns the ought, as the demand of a being that was already there before the demand, and did not first have to wait for it. But is the being that faith rejects, then, one and the same with the being that science finds, and the ought that faith holds out one and the same with the ought that science subordinates? It requires in fact only a serious glance to recognize that in this supposed difference as well, as in all differences, the accord of the cognition of faith with the cognition of reason, supposedly different from it, only the more proves itself. The being that faith condemns as our present state is precisely our human, sinful being, the being-for-self, and with it the unactuality of our being, non-being. The ought that it holds out to us is the admonition to the being originally bestowed upon us, which we owe, because through our guilt we have forfeited the good entrusted to us, the demand to enter again into this being, which is lacking to us, but not to itself, but not the demand first to make this being. The being, on the other hand, which reason raises above the ought, and intuits as independent of it, is precisely the actual [p. 181] being from which we have fallen, without its being for that reason any less actual in and for itself. And the ought, which is so contemptuously rejected and mocked, is the fancy that being took heed of it in order to be, as though being, because it is lacking to us, were not there at all, and were waiting precisely for us, until we make it. Reason acknowledges the ought only insofar as this acknowledges being as already actually existing, and refers man, who is not in it, to this as to the present actuality. If this clarification concerning the different meaning of the same words is not yet sufficient to settle the above difference, we hold ourselves more closely to the content of the Christian faith itself, which seems to accuse philosophy on account of that difference. The Christian faith is nothing other than faith in Christ, that is, faith in Him who first for us, and thereupon also in us, fulfills the law, transfigures the ought into willing, willing into deed, and thus into being, and consequently sublates it. If in this the faith in the Gospel proves itself the end of the law, it cannot escape offence and misunderstanding from the world. And yet it should make itself guilty, toward the science of reason, of this very misunderstanding under which it must suffer in the world, if the latter directs its whole essence, all its meditating and perceiving, away from the ought-to-be, and toward the actual being that is held out to us, in order to invite us to accept it as a gift of grace, and thereby to discharge the claims that we owed, but could not fulfil? Indeed language has one word for guilt and ought—ὀφείλειν, debere—and Scripture teaches us, in the light of revelation, the connection between sin and law, between guilt and indebtedness—ὀφείλημα, debitum. We are not what we [p. 182] ought to be, but what we are not, that we ought to be, that we are bound to be, only because we are guilty of not actually being, because through our guilt we have incurred the loss of the being entrusted to us. So Scripture teaches, and so we believe. And if now, accordingly, the relations of being and ought develop themselves in the Concept, if reason, as existing, gives the honor to being as actually existing, and on the other hand refers the ought back to its position, how should we be able to mistake what is thereby said, how should we not recognize again in the Concept what we already had and comprehended in representation? And does not experience daily teach that this ought, which should remind us daily of our guilt and indebtedness, conversely turns into the most insufferable arrogance, in that man, to whom the law is given in order to obey, makes himself the lawgiver, or, instead of accepting what is prepared for him, imagines that he must first himself make the being that he is to receive again. With this, then, this difference too, which wears itself out on the ought, is sufficiently settled. For the rest, all these differences in their one-sided conception are as little to be laid to the charge of the cognition of faith as of the cognition of reason, for we have come to know the unity of both; but they fall equally to the charge of philosophy, as it must let itself be deformed in individual subjects, if not as a whole, yet in particular respects, and to that of faith, when in individual subjects, if not as a whole, yet in certain directions, it is infected and clouded by sin. And in what sinner is reason, in what sinner faith, wholly pure, and always pure? But enough of separating and uniting! From the identity winding itself everywhere through the difference it is explained at the same time how it comes about that to us so often in the simple confession of faith [p. 183] of a living Christian the deepest result of speculative philosophy is met with, and in the most remote philosophemes the children’s doctrine of the catechism. Hence it also comes about that everything that runs counter to the Christian faith and contradicts biblical revelation is also rejected by philosophy, and that where revelation is silent, philosophy too is at an end. As identity has everywhere asserted itself, so too the true state of affairs concerning the difference has everywhere come to light. This difference bears the common lot of all those oppositions which are members of one organic whole, in which the identity of being and non-being reveals itself, in that they are just as much as they are not. For this very reason it has been impossible to find such a difference as could hold faith and knowing apart as two different and yet independent modes of cognition and of life, for we could not, individual aberrations aside, think living faith without thinking and knowing, with which it is essentially connected, nor thinking and knowing without faith, as the sole foundation and reality of all knowing, nor faith without activity, thinking without suffering, nor content without form, not without the form essential to it, nor form without content, not without the content identical with the form. When it has been said: “Philosophy cannot believe; it would annihilate itself through faith,” or “it is just as certain that philosophy does not believe as that faith does not philosophize,”—does not think, we have seen how these and similar pronouncements settle themselves and turn about, for we found that all philosophy has the object, and with it faith, as its foundation, and without faith would annihilate itself, would evaporate in unactual Ideas, and that conversely faith [p. 184] recognizes thought as its essence, that both, in order to be, mutually quicken, govern, and enlighten one another. All philosophy believes, as surely as it seeks and finds ground, faith thinks, as surely as it subsists in the spiritual life. Philosophia, obiter libata, a Deo abducit, penitus hausta, reducit ad eundem [Philosophy, sipped lightly, leads away from God; drunk deeply, leads back to Him]. What holds for superficial, half philosophy, for non-philosophy, does not touch philosophy itself. But why so many words? Who denies, then, that true philosophy leads to God, and so far goes one way with faith, has one ground? When we take the field against philosophy, we mean not the true philosophy, but the false, which is the ruling philosophy, the philosophy of the day. Nevertheless you contend against philosophy as such. Why, then, do you not say that you contend against sham philosophy, against non-philosophy? Something lies behind that. All actual philosophy is true philosophy. Why, then, do you call that philosophy which is non-philosophy? Why do you call untrue philosophy philosophy? Why else than because actual philosophy, the philosophy of the Concept, seems to you untrue? It is in fact already to be feared from this, what will presently be confirmed in detail, that you persecute precisely the true philosophy, as the actual. And this we all indeed do only too easily, now because its thoughts are not our thoughts, now because its thoughts are turned and twisted by the understanding into other thoughts. “True philosophy,” so many opponents of philosophy confess, “true philosophy is inseparable from religion, indeed it is, rightly understood, itself religion, which, when it fills our life, leads to the cognition of God, but—only by the practical way.” Why this But? Is, then, this practical [p. 185] way not essential to philosophy, and belonging to its very own Concept? Is philosophy even conceivable without this practical way? But how they mean it soon becomes clear to us, for the same opponents at once declare themselves again against thought, against the real Concept, in which precisely the practical way comes to light. “Thinking,” they say, “is neither the element of religion nor that of virtue, but the element of religion is a pure heart,” as if this heart were not also the element of thinking. “Not to the pure Concept,” they say, “but only to the pure heart is God accessible.” Thus not to the spirit itself, not to the whole human essence reborn out of the Spirit, but only to a fraction of man, made in thought by abstraction? “Not the understanding,” they say further, “not thinking, nor yet the heart, is what leads to truth in the highest sense, but the sacrifice of the heart.” To be sure, it is not merely the sacrifice of one’s own heart, but also the sacrifice of one’s own understanding, out of which spirit is reborn as the identity of heart and understanding, and on which all faith rests, but on which all philosophy too has rested from of old. Faith and philosophy thrive toward actuality the more, the more decided, complete, and faithful the sacrifice is; the less is sacrificed, the weaker and more incomplete are faith and knowing. If in no man philosophy has always been wholly pure and faithful, so too here below no faith remains without strife and temptation. But our opponents, beloved in the Lord, do the utmost when they presume and say: “As little as God can be laid hold of with hands, so little can he be apprehended with the Concept.” This simile is to beat philosophy from the field at one stroke. Philosophy answers just as briefly with [p. 186] the testimony of the disciple whom the Lord loves: As surely as God—the Word that was from the beginning, the Word of life—has let himself be beheld with our eyes and touched with our hands, so surely He does not withdraw himself from the Concept either, whereby the Spirit, as being in Him, cognizes Him. As surely as God imparts himself in the holy sacraments, according to his promise, through visible and palpable elements, and lets himself be enjoyed in these elements, so surely is God Spirit, who in the flesh imparts himself actually and essentially to the flesh, as to the body of the spirit, and hence to the spirit, to the Concept—not to the abstract Concept.— Where such misunderstandings assert themselves, and seek to take a place even among the brethren in Christ, there many and lengthy words are indeed not superfluous in order to defend the identity of speculative philosophy of religion with the Christian cognition of faith. Indeed, it is precisely now time to draw attention to this in general and in particular, because the light, loose, cold times are just now passing, which sought to dispose of the whole heavy and rich import of Christian dogmatics and symbolics, which runs through all Christian centuries, in the manner of Erasmus, as scholastic subtleties, as dry formulas and useless brooding, without being touched in the least by the inwardness and fidelity of the diligence, by the unmistakable earnestness of the contemplation, by the love and depth in the inquiry, by the holy awe and the strict obedience in the stiff formulas and standing predicates. But whoever has taken even single glimpses into this rich world of spirit will soon stand still in wonder, and look on with joy at how the Lord builds his Church through all the centuries, and how at all times the disciples of Jesus dwell at each word in the Word of God, follow up every hint, unfold in every truth its inexhaustible wealth on all sides and in all relations, in every image [p. 187] besides its general meaning also pursue its actuality, develop the interpretation according to every sense that lets the word itself stand unfalsified, and bring together all the treasures of the Bible, in order to carry out the system down to the smallest parts, down to the finest veins—all in order more and more to appropriate the rich Word, as the power of God, to live ever more deeply into it, and with all the senses to imbibe it ever more firmly into all the pores.∗) Or are we really still now to think that such intercourse with God, because it first sets thought in motion, should leave the heart cold, and the hands with which we act lie slack and quiet in the lap? Of all the words of Holy Scripture none is superfluous, for all Scripture, inspired by God, is profitable for teaching, for reproof, for improvement, for discipline in righteousness.—— So much for peace between faith and knowing, which, as knowing, can dispense with the closer designation “true knowing,” because all knowing is true, as all faith is, for superstition is not faith. Nevertheless the difference between faith and knowing cannot be denied, identity does not exclude difference, and in the error that we have demonstrated in the differences there lies truth too; but this difference is only not to be grasped as if we could stop at its abstractions, We have already several times thought to have come to the end of the perpetual process of distinguishing, but as often as we suppose we are finished with it, so often new differences arise again, or at least new relations, in which differences already dismissed renew themselves and return with intensified force. In this way, however, we can never be finished, unless we renounce this endless casuistry and refer back once and for all to the principles in which its dismissal and settlement lie. Only one difference must we still hear, because it is only too often repeated and urged against philosophy. It concerns the ought, and will also settle itself in the concept of the ought. ∗) The speculative content in what the newer “Enlightenment” calls the “scholastic rubbish of the old dogmatics” was acknowledged by Schelling too, at a time when he still found the content of the first books of religion themselves “meagre,” and seemed to share the astonishment of the Indians, who did not dispute the Incarnation of God in Christ, but “merely found it strange that among the Christians there had happened only once what among them occurred often and in constant repetition.” Lectures on the Method of Academic Study, pp. 193, 198.

e: [p. 188] just as if one subject could live merely in faith, another merely in knowing,—but rather in such a way that in each mode the other indeed finds itself and distinguishes itself, but also at the same time knows itself as inseparably bound. Hence we need only hold all the individual differences quite rigidly and sharply apart from one another, and set them against each other, in order to see them vanish in one relation after another. Thinking and faith are therefore to be regarded as parts of one living whole, which are not self-subsistent for themselves, so that as separated they cannot maintain themselves in actuality, and, nevertheless separated, turn into distorted images of the holiest. “Only by mutually permeating each other can the essence make itself known.” Both distinguish themselves as consciousness and existence, the same being belongs to both, but being is not actual unless it is consciousness. Properly, then, we deny less the difference than the separation. Hence faith too is not to be separated from philosophy without annihilating it, and if in most recent times the dispute has even been renewed whether a Christian philosophy is possible, which is indeed strange enough, since it has been actual since the oldest times,—but sham philosophy does not trouble itself about actuality,—then on the contrary it is to be asserted that no philosophy other than Christian is possible, as indeed none is actual. In the so-called heathen philosophy of antiquity, as well as in the not so-called heathen philosophy of later times and of our own, only so much is true as is Christian. To separate philosophy from Christianity is therefore in fact nothing other than to divorce it from its content and purpose, namely from truth. Such a separation is a divorce: divorce presupposes adultery, a complete falling out with the truth, shipwreck of faith and of knowing.

e: [p. 189] The Apostle Paul too seems to acknowledge as well as to sublate the much-discussed difference when he says: “I know in whom I believe!” Happy are we if we can say it after him with a good conscience, for it is a precious thing that the heart be made firm; and it becomes firm and certain only when it knows in whom it believes. In dem zweyten Abschnitte der vorstehenden Schrift iſt. nur Beyspielsweise an einzelnen vorzüglich verfänglichen Lehren der speculativen Philosophie deren Verſtändigung, und an einzelnen besonders häufigen Vorurtheilen und Mißverständnissen über dieselbe deren Wiederlegung der Vorstellung näher gebracht worden. Eben deswegen konnte es auf eine Vollständigkeit des Inhalts nicht abgesehn, sondern nur um Winke zum weitern Verständnisse zu thun seyn. Indessen ist ein Beyspiel unerwähnt geblieben, welches sich zu jenen Zwecken besonders geeignet haben würde, da es selbst innerhalb der Schule dieser Philosophie durch deren Formalismus zu Mißverständnissen Nahrung erhält, wodurch es mit der heiligen Schrift und der Kirche in Opposition zu treten scheint. Der Formalismus dieser Philosophie bezeichnet nämlich, nicht ohne Gefahr Abstractionen und concrete Vorstellungen in einander zu mischen und zu verwirren, den ursprünglichen Zustand des Menschen in und nach der Schöpfung als Ansichſeyn, hingegen den Zustand durch den Fall und nach dem Falle als Fürsichseyn, als Bewußtseyn der Trennung von Gott, des Zwiespalts zwischen dem Subjecte und Objecte, als Erkenntniß des Guten und Bösen, hiermit als Dualismus des Ansichseyns und Fürsichseyns, endlich aber den Zustand durch die Erlösung als Rückkehr zu der ursprünglichen Einheit, mit dem Unterschiede, daß diese aus dem indifferenten Ansichseyn zum An- und Fürsichseyn erhoben und verklärt wird.
e: […] […] Afterword. In the second section of the foregoing work it was only by way of example, in the case of a few particularly captious doctrines of speculative philosophy, that their being understood, and, in the case of a few especially frequent prejudices and misunderstandings about it, their refutation, were brought closer to representation. For that very reason no completeness of content could be aimed at, but only hints toward further understanding. Meanwhile one example has remained unmentioned which would have been especially suited to those purposes, since even within the school of this philosophy it receives nourishment for misunderstandings through its formalism, whereby it appears to enter into opposition with Holy Scripture and the Church. The formalism of this philosophy, namely, designates—not without danger of mixing and confusing abstractions and concrete representations with one another—the original state of man in and after creation as being-in-itself, the state through the Fall and after the Fall, on the other hand, as being-for-self, as consciousness of the separation from God, of the discord between subject and object, as cognition of good and evil, hence as the dualism of being-in-itself and being-for-self, but finally the state through redemption as the return to the original unity, with the difference that this is raised and transfigured from the indifferent being-in-itself to being-in-and-for-itself.

e: [p. 191] From these formulas, raw and dead as they are at first, there results, however, with sensuous apprehension and handling, only too easily, not only outside the school but partly within it as well, the same unscriptural view of the Fall and of the state that preceded it, which we find expressed in the critical philosophy, namely in Kant∗) and Schiller∗∗), and with which we believed ourselves at least philosophically done, though it has kept its currency in the domain of unbelief. Indeed, this current view seems, in the way in which the Master of the speculative philosophy of our time has still recently expressed himself on it [in the Yearbooks for Scientific Criticism. June 1828. Nos. 105, 106. p. 841.], to have obtained a confirmation very welcome to rationalism. If God, as the good, as that which is, on the one hand, and man, as the nothing, as evil, on the other hand, are merely presupposed, then “there is lacking here,” in the Master’s own words, “the moment of creation in general, and of man in particular according to God’s likeness, and from there on of the transition from this merely original, merely in-itself unity of human nature with the divine, which has not yet entered into existence, to what is expressed as the semblance or the nothing. The semblance determines itself to the more concrete, which is consciousness and freedom, and the difficulty is that this semblance contains not only the source of evil, the eating, falling away from the likeness, from the tree of cognition [p. 192] of good and evil, but also the principle of the return to the likeness; so that God himself is introduced saying: Behold, Adam has become like one of Us, and knows what is good and evil (Gen. 3:22)—the passage which constitutes the other side to the first meaning of cognizing, and which is usually far too little considered in its depth, indeed is customarily scarcely even noticed.”∗) What are we to say to this? and how are we to bring the abstract Concept nearer to representation? So much is certain first of all, that man, as he is now, as he is after the Fall, not as he was created but as he is born, is at first only in itself, that is, lies in a deep, dull sleep of sin, without cognizing good and evil, without distinguishing subject and object, without bringing to consciousness the separation from God and the discord of his essence. As he awakens to consciousness, he is for himself, and now substance and subject step apart, and over to different sides. This self-consciousness develops gradually, and indeed first as consciousness of difference in general, in which the sleep of sin as such continues even after the awakening, and thereafter as consciousness of the cause of this discord, cognition of sin and pain of sin. Self-consciousness becomes consciousness of guilt, and with this the state of unblessedness, upon which finally follows redemption out of this discord, and the consciousness of it, whereby being, split into in-itself and for-itself, is transfigured into being-in-and-for-itself. This is the course of the human essence after the Fall, and in accordance with divine revelation. It is further in accordance with Scripture that the original state of innocence and divine likeness is torn apart by sin, but through redemption is not merely restored but exalted and glorified more than before. Heb. 2:16, 11; 2 Cor. 3:18; Luke 15:7. Insofar the Fall, against the intention of the devil, but in accordance with his specious promises, has become in God’s hands the means of glorifying God in man still more. What the serpent promises in order to deceive, Gen. 3:5, that God confirms, Gen. 3:22, 7, in order to deprive the deception of its force, and to corroborate the truth that lies in the deception against its knowledge and will. Whereby it wants to corrupt man, thereby is he, contrary to merit and worthiness, glorified. And what is there to object to this, if the representations of the two states, the original and the last, perfected state, are designated in the Concept as being-in-itself and being-in-and-for-itself? whereby they are distinguished not only from the state of sin torn apart in being-for-self, but also from one another as the lower and the higher. Only that this being-in-itself, in which man was created, is also to be distinguished from that being-in-itself in which he is born. The difference consists in this, that there the separation from God is not yet, here is not known, there innocence, here ignorance. The original being-in-itself is childhood, but not the childhood that we now see before our eyes, although traces of that childhood are still left over in this one, only disfigured. Mark 10:14. Thus this unstained being-in-itself is divine likeness, which does not exclude the transformation into the same image from one radiance to another. It is no less in accordance with Scripture that man is nothing, nothing before the Fall, nothing after the Fall. But this nothing and that nothing are not the same nothing. There he is nothing, because what he is is not he, but God in him, here he is nothing,—because he is no longer in God, and through being-for-self has stepped out of what is. And what is there to object to this, if this annihilation of the original nothing proves itself to be self-affirmation, since we cannot deny that sin consists in self-emancipation, and has had unhappy self-consciousness as its consequence. Through the annihilation of the original nothing man has indeed attained self-subsistence, only that this, for itself, is vain semblance and nothing, hence it again requires another nothing, in order to sublate the sinful nothing and to preserve it in being-in-and-for-itself. It is a harsh expression when it is said that in the Fall the principle of redemption is already given, but nothing else can be understood by this than that from it the seed is to proceed that puts an end to sin and crushes the serpent’s head. Now it is also explained that Adam first entered into existence through sin, insofar as only thereby did he attain separate existence, whereas before it was not he, but God in him. If, accordingly, sin is regarded on the one hand as Fall, on the other as a moment of development, it is not to be overlooked that that side belongs to man, whose guilt therefore is not to be excused or justified, but this side, on the other hand, pertains to God, whom sin must serve, according to Scripture, as a means for development. Scripture also teaches that God foresaw the Fall, and prepared redemption from eternity. Eph. 3:11; 1:4. Error arises only when this consideration in any way becomes a temptation to justify man in his sin, and to lighten the heavy weight of inborn and personal sin. This error is not to be laid to the charge of speculation, which consists rather in this, that it discovers the truth in the unscriptural error which extols the Fall of mankind as a giant stride of the same toward perfection, and which cannot be refuted in any other way than by acknowledging the truth hidden beneath it and vindicating it for the highest Being, because it is his deed and not mankind’s, but redounds to the latter’s good.
